title: Getting around
goal: Buy the right ticket to Seaview and find out how to get to the platform.
twist: The ticket machine does not accept your card, so you ask a person for help.
note: Fictional dialogue constructed for teaching purposes. Harbour City and Seaview are fictional places.

start.speaker: Narrator
start.line: You want to go to Seaview for the day. The ticket machine shows: CARD NOT ACCEPTED. There is a help desk next to the machines.

greet.speaker: Sam
greet.line: Hi there. Are you OK? Can I help?

options.text: Excuse me, can you help me? My card doesn't work in the machine.
options.feedback: Clear and polite. You got attention and explained the problem in one short sentence.

options.text: Your machine is broken. Fix it.
options.feedback: The grammar is fine, but it sounds like an order and like you blame Sam. Staff help more happily when you ask, not tell.
options.recast: Excuse me, the machine doesn't take my card. Can you help me?

options.text: I have problem card machine.
options.feedback: Sam can guess, but it is hard to understand. Use a full sentence with a verb: 'My card doesn't work in the machine.'
options.recast: I have a problem: my card doesn't work in the machine.

blunt.speaker: Sam
blunt.line: Well, I can't fix it myself, I'm afraid. But I can sell you a ticket here at the desk.

guess.speaker: Sam
guess.line: Sorry, the machine doesn't take your card? OK, no problem. I can sell you a ticket here.

help.speaker: Sam
help.line: So, where would you like to go today?
help.spell: Seaview: S, E, A, V, I, E, W.

build.prompt: Ask for a ticket to Seaview. You are coming back this evening.

nearMisses.feedback: A single is a one-way ticket. You are coming back this evening, so you need a return.
A single is a one-way ticket. You are coming back this evening, so you need a return.

build.hint: Start with 'A ...'. Choose the ticket type, then the place, then 'please'.

options.text: A return to Seaview, please. I'm coming back this evening.
options.feedback: Perfect. You named the ticket type and the place, and the reason helps Sam choose the right fare.

options.text: Seaview. Give me a ticket.
options.feedback: Correct English, but 'Give me' sounds rude in a shop or station. Also, Sam still doesn't know which ticket you need.

options.text: I want go to Seaview and come back today evening.
options.feedback: Sam understands, but there are two common errors: 'want to go' (not 'want go') and 'this evening' (not 'today evening').
options.recast: I want to go to Seaview and come back this evening.

singlereturn.speaker: Sam
singlereturn.line: Sure. A single or a return?
singlereturn.slower: One way, or there and back?

options.text: A return, please. I'm coming back this evening.
options.feedback: Good. 'Return' is the right word for a ticket there and back.

options.text: I don't care. Just the cheapest one.
options.feedback: Asking for the cheapest is fine, but 'I don't care' sounds rude. And a cheap single would not get you home.
options.recast: Which one is cheaper for a day trip?

options.text: Return. I come back in the evening today.
options.feedback: Sam understands 'return'. For a plan, use 'I'm coming back' (present continuous) and say 'this evening'.
options.recast: A return. I'm coming back this evening.

recast-return.speaker: Sam
recast-return.line: So you want a return to Seaview, coming back this evening? No problem.

price.speaker: Sam
price.line: That's eleven forty for an off-peak day return. The next train is at ten fifteen.
price.slower: It's eleven forty. Off-peak means a cheaper time. The train is at ten fifteen.
price.spell: Off-peak: O, F, F, then peak: P, E, A, K.

options.text: Can I pay by card here?
options.feedback: Good question. The machine didn't take your card, so you check before you pay.

options.text: Sorry, what does 'off-peak' mean?
options.feedback: Great repair strategy. Asking about one word is quick and normal.

options.text: Eleven forty? That's too expensive.
options.feedback: You can say a price is high, but here it sounds like a complaint to the wrong person. Sam does not set the prices.
options.recast: OK, is that the cheapest ticket?

options.text: I can pay with card?
options.feedback: Sam understands — a rising question like this is fine in speech. The usual phrase is 'by card': 'Can I pay by card?' Starting with 'Can I' is also clearer and more polite.

offpeak.speaker: Sam
offpeak.line: Off-peak means outside the busy times, so it's cheaper. You can travel after half past nine.

pricey.speaker: Sam
pricey.line: I know, it's a lot. The off-peak return is the cheapest one, though.

paid.speaker: Sam
paid.line: Yes, of course. Just tap it here. ... That's gone through. Here's your ticket.
paid.slower: Yes. Put your card here. OK, it worked. This is your ticket.

options.text: Thanks. Which platform does it leave from?
options.feedback: Good. You thanked Sam and asked for the next thing you need.

options.text: OK. Bye.
options.feedback: Not wrong, but very short. And you don't know where the train is yet.
options.recast: Thanks a lot. Which platform is it?

options.text: Which platform it leaves?
options.feedback: A very common error. Questions with 'which' need 'does': 'Which platform does it leave from?'
options.recast: Which platform does it leave from?

wait.speaker: Sam
wait.line: Wait, before you go! Do you know where your train is?

platform.speaker: Sam
platform.line: It leaves from platform four. Go straight on, past the café, then turn left. The stairs are on your right.
platform.slower: Platform four. Go straight. Pass the café. Turn left. The stairs are on the right.
platform.spell: Four: F, O, U, R. Platform number four.

options.text: So straight on, then left, and the stairs are on the right. Is that right?
options.feedback: Excellent. You checked your understanding by repeating the key steps.

options.text: Great. How long does it take to get to Seaview?
options.feedback: A useful question. It helps you plan your day.

options.text: No need to explain. I will find it myself.
options.feedback: Correct English, but it sounds like you didn't want Sam's help. 'Thanks, I'll find it' is friendlier.
options.recast: Thanks, I think I can find it.

options.text: I am understand. Thank you.
options.feedback: Don't use 'am' with 'understand'. Say 'I understand' or, even more natural, 'Got it, thanks.'

confirm.speaker: Sam
confirm.line: That's right. Platform four. The journey takes about forty minutes.

journey.speaker: Sam
journey.line: About forty minutes. It's a nice trip along the coast. Remember: platform four, straight on, then left.

fine.speaker: Sam
fine.line: OK. It's well signed. Look for platform four.

options.text: Thanks very much for your help.
options.feedback: A warm, natural way to finish. People remember a friendly thank-you.

options.text: Yes.
options.feedback: 'Yes' does not answer 'Have a good trip!' Say 'Thanks!' or 'Thank you, you too.'

options.text: Thank you for your helping.
options.feedback: Use the noun 'help': 'Thank you for your help.'

end.speaker: Narrator
end.line: You have a return ticket to Seaview and you know the way to platform four.
end.summary: Task complete: right ticket, payment solved, directions understood.
